site.name: Luc Desautels
site.tagline: My main focus right now is in robotics, however I also rock climb, play fiddle, and have a passion for drone photography.

slides.title: Intro to Sailfish
slides.body: A proof of technology for a low-cost, autonomous marine search and rescue drone. We set out to reduce the time and cost for Coast Guard and volunteer rescue to make first visual contact.
slides.longBody: Project Sailfish is a proof of technology for a low-cost, autonomous marine search and rescue drone. We set out to reduce the time and cost for Coast Guard and volunteer rescue crews to make first visual contact with a person in the water. Three generations of prototypes — each a step closer to a system that any rescue org could fly without a manufacturer in the loop.
slides.caption: Sailfish Gen.3 · field test, Lake Ontario

slides.title: Letter from the Airforce Foundation
slides.body: Recognition from the CEO of the Airforce Foundation, endorsed by a Navy Captain who has advised the Chief of Defense Staff.
slides.longBody: The Air Force Foundation's CEO wrote a personal endorsement of Sailfish, co-signed by a retired Navy Captain who has advised the Canadian Chief of Defense Staff. They specifically called out the cost ceiling, the open-source release, and the relevance to volunteer SAR units operating without dedicated air assets.
slides.caption: Endorsement letter · scanned original

slides.title: My Technical Work
slides.body: Deep experience in mechanical design and simulation, electrical engineering, and software for autonomous systems across three generations of prototypes.
slides.longBody: Across three generations I owned: fuselage CAD and CFRP layup planning; the 5.8 GHz video stack tuned for over-water multipath; a thrust-stand campaign that fed motor/prop selection; and the autonomy loop running spiral-search paths on a Pixhawk + companion compute. Each generation traded weight, range, and complexity differently and the lessons stacked.
slides.caption: Exploded view · CAD generation 3

slides.title: Leadership and Entrepreneurship
slides.body: Founded and led a team of 6 high school students. Engaged Coast Guard personnel, university professors, and industry experts to shape requirements and direction.
slides.longBody: I founded the project and led a team of 6 high schoolers across two design cycles. I built the relationships that turned this from a school project into something credible: interviews with Coast Guard auxiliary crews, professors at Waterloo and UofT, and industry mentors. The team has shipped peer-reviewed write-ups and won two local engineering awards.
slides.caption: Team standup · Toronto workshop

slides.title: Open Sourced
slides.body: Open sourced the project to share our learnings and enable others working on similar problems in the drone and SAR communities.
slides.longBody: The full design — CAD, firmware, build notes, and the lessons from each generation — is published openly. The goal is for any volunteer SAR unit, university lab, or hobbyist team to be able to pick up where we left off without re-deriving the basics. The repo has been mirrored on a few Coast Guard auxiliary servers.
slides.caption: GitHub repository · public release

slides.title: Intro to FTC
slides.body: Five years in FIRST Tech Challenge competitive robotics — two years learning the basics, one doing mechanical-electrical chassis design, and two as a mentor.
slides.longBody: Five years in FIRST Tech Challenge — two years learning the basics on a rookie team, one year owning the mechanical-electrical chassis as a builder, and two years as a mentor on Team 16366. FTC is where I learned to ship under deadline pressure with a rotating cast of teammates, and it's where I figured out I like teaching the craft as much as doing it.
slides.caption: Team 16366 · Ontario Championship 2024

slides.title: Inspire Award and Worlds
slides.body: Placed #1 in the 2024 FTC Ontario Championships (Inspire Award) and went on to represent Canada at the world championships in Houston, Texas.
slides.longBody: Inspire is FTC's top award — judges across engineering, outreach, and team culture pick one team out of the province. We won it in 2024 and represented Ontario at the world championship in Houston, Texas. That trip was a benchmark: we saw what world-class teams look like and came home with a sharper picture of what's possible.
slides.caption: Inspire Award · Ontario Championship

slides.title: My Work on Mechanical
slides.body: Worked on important sub-assemblies including the custom CNC chassis and arm transfer system. Learnt quickly through hands-on projects.
slides.longBody: I owned the CNC chassis plate from concept through fixturing and ops — my first time taking a part all the way from CAD into manufacturing. I also designed the two-stage arm transfer system that gave us a passive deadband and made our autonomous routines a lot more reliable. Both subsystems are documented as build references for the rookie team.
slides.caption: CNC chassis plate · finishing pass

slides.title: Mentoring and Team Building
slides.body: Continued as a mentor giving insights on design and leadership challenges. Teaching peers and writing documentation to transfer skills to younger team members.
slides.longBody: After my competing years I stayed on as a mentor for two seasons. My focus has been writing design and leadership documentation that survives team turnover — onboarding decks, manufacturing checklists, and lessons-learned from past seasons. I want the rookies who join next year to start two months ahead of where I started.
slides.caption: Design review · winter build

slides.title: Outreach Projects
slides.body: Girl Guide STEM seminars, 3D printer workshops, teaching in grade 5 design club, and curating bilingual self-study STEM resources.
slides.longBody: Outreach is one of the reasons our team wins Inspire. I've run Girl Guide STEM seminars, hands-on 3D printer workshops at the local makerspace, design club sessions for grade 5 students, and I curate a bilingual self-study STEM resource collection that gets shared with families looking for after-school enrichment.

engPrograms.title: FIRST® Tech Challenge
engPrograms.blurb: Four competition seasons with the TFS Robotic Unicorns, most of it on the mechanical side — drivetrain, manipulators, and the fixturing needed to make each part twice. FTC deadlines are unforgiving, so the work is biased toward parts a student can machine on a school 3-axis and repair between matches.
engPrograms.caption: Team 16366 · competition build

skills.title: CNC machining & fixturing
skills.desc: Cut the drive chassis from 6061 on the school's 3-axis, with soft jaws that made the second copy repeatable.
skills.long: The first chassis took a full weekend and came out 0.4 mm out of square. The fix was less about the toolpath than the workholding: a set of soft jaws cut in place, plus a tab-and-drop scheme so the plate stayed rigid until the final pass. After that, a replacement plate was a two-hour job — which mattered the one time we snapped one at a qualifier.

skills.title: Arm & transfer mechanism
skills.desc: A two-stage arm that hands the game element off to the scoring mechanism without a driver having to line it up.
skills.long: The transfer is the part of an FTC robot that eats match time. We built a two-stage arm with a passive hand-off: the geometry forces the element into the same seat every cycle, so the driver only has to be roughly right. Getting there took three revisions of the claw geometry and a hard look at where the compliance should live.

skills.title: Autonomous routine pathing
skills.desc: Tuned the 30-second autonomous path so it scored reliably from either alliance side instead of only on a good day.
skills.long: Autonomous is worth a lot of points and is where most rookie teams lose them. Rather than chase a perfect single path, we built the routine around checkpoints the robot could recover from — so a slightly-off approach still finished the cycle instead of stalling. Repeatability over peak score.

images.caption: Robot running auto on the practice field

skills.title: Iterative CAD & design review
skills.desc: Ran the design in CAD first and reviewed it with the team before anything got cut, which killed most of the expensive mistakes.
skills.long: Every subsystem went through a full assembly in CAD with the real hardware modelled — motors, bearings, the actual extrusion — so interference showed up on screen instead of on the machine. The review itself mattered as much as the model: walking three other builders through the assembly caught things I'd stopped seeing.

skills.title: Onboarding & team documentation
skills.desc: Wrote the rookie handbook the team still onboards with, so a new builder can be useful in a week instead of a season.
skills.long: Most of what a rookie needs isn't in the FTC manual — it's the local knowledge about which tool lives where and why we do a thing a certain way. I wrote it down: a handbook covering the shop, the CAD conventions, and the first build task a new member should own. It's the reason the team survives graduating classes.

engPrograms.title: Project Sailfish
engPrograms.blurb: A low-cost autonomous marine search-and-rescue drone, built to cut the time and cost for rescue crews to make first visual contact with a person in the water. Three generations of airframe, and with them most of the disciplines below — composites, RF, propulsion, CAD, and the software that ties them together.
engPrograms.caption: Sailfish Gen.3 · field test, Lake Ontario

skills.title: Advanced materials manufacturing
skills.desc: Laid up foam-core composite floats that survive a hard water landing and still let the airframe fly.
skills.long: A marine drone has to land on water and be flyable afterwards. The floats are foam-core with a glass skin — light enough not to wreck the weight budget, stiff enough to take the slam load. Getting the layup schedule right took several test articles and a lot of deliberately abusive landings.

skills.title: Long-range video transmission
skills.desc: Characterised 5.8 GHz analog video over open water, where the reflection off the surface eats the link budget.
skills.long: Open water is a mirror at 5.8 GHz: the surface bounce arrives out of phase with the direct path and the picture drops out at ranges that work fine over land. I measured it properly — range sweeps at several altitudes, antenna polarisations compared — and the result changed where the antenna sits on the airframe and how high we fly the search pattern.

skills.title: Advanced 3D design & assembly
skills.desc: Designed the wing carry-through that takes the whole flight load through a joint you can still pull apart in the field.
skills.long: The carry-through is the highest-stress joint on the aircraft and it also has to come apart for transport — those two requirements fight. The answer was a carbon spar through a machined saddle, with the fasteners loaded in shear rather than pulling on the composite. Modelled as a full assembly so the tolerance stack was visible before anything was cut.

skills.title: Avionics packaging — VTX stack
skills.desc: Packed transmitter, camera and DC-DC into the nose cone without pushing the centre of gravity aft of the spar.
skills.long: Three competing nose layouts, judged on CG, cooling and antenna isolation. The winner buries the VTX heat-sink in the airflow channel, keeps the antenna two wavelengths off the carbon spar, and lets the camera tilt 22° forward without recutting the fuselage. A thermal mock-up with a dummy heat load settled the cooling question before committing.

images.caption: VTX + camera stack, nose cone open
CG balance check on the bench

skills.title: Tilt-rotor control electronics
skills.desc: Built the controller that hands the aircraft between hover and forward flight without dropping it.
skills.long: The transition is the dangerous part of any tilt-rotor: for a few seconds the aircraft is neither a quadcopter nor a plane and the control authority moves between surfaces. The controller blends the two mixers across the tilt angle rather than switching at a threshold, which is what stopped the nose-drop we kept seeing on early flights.

images.caption: Bench test of the transition blend

skills.title: Aerodynamic analysis — CFD & tuft testing
skills.desc: Ran CFD on the wing, then taped tufts to the real one to find out where the simulation was lying.
skills.long: CFD gets you a plausible pressure distribution and a false sense of certainty. Tufts on the actual wing, filmed through a speed sweep, showed separation starting earlier and further inboard than the model predicted — traceable to a surface finish the simulation had no way to know about. The washout got adjusted off the tuft data, not the CFD.

skills.title: Propulsion characterisation
skills.desc: Built a thrust stand to measure motor and prop combinations instead of trusting the manufacturer's numbers.
skills.long: Published prop data is optimistic and rarely measured at the RPM you actually fly. The stand measures thrust, current and RPM together so efficiency comes out in grams per watt across the real operating range. Two of the combinations we were about to buy turned out to be meaningfully worse than the cheaper option.

skills.title: Battery pack fabrication
skills.desc: Spot-welded 6S Li-ion packs sized to the mission profile, with the balance leads routed so they survive vibration.
skills.long: Off-the-shelf packs are sized for hobby flights, not a 20-minute search leg. Building our own meant choosing the cell for the discharge curve we actually needed and welding it properly — nickel strip, spot welder, no soldering directly to cans. The failure mode we designed against was a balance lead chafing through in flight, so the routing and strain relief got as much attention as the cells.

skills.title: Search-pattern optimisation
skills.desc: Worked out the spiral spacing that covers the most probable water in the least time, given the camera we actually have.
skills.long: The search pattern is a coverage problem constrained by the camera's real detection range on a person in water — which is much shorter than the sensor's nominal range once you account for chop and glare. Tightening the spiral to that number, rather than the datasheet number, changes total search time considerably. The output is the flight plan the ground station loads.

skills.title: Ground station & telemetry
skills.desc: Wrote the operator interface a rescue volunteer can run without a manufacturer on the phone.
skills.long: The whole point of Sailfish is that a rescue organisation can fly it themselves, which makes the ground station a hard requirement rather than a nicety. It shows the search pattern, the live video and the aircraft state on one screen, and it is deliberately boring: no mode the operator can get lost in, and the abort is always in the same place.

images.caption: Station set up in the field

engPrograms.title: Uncategorized
engPrograms.blurb: The work that doesn't belong to a program. Some of it is infrastructure I run because I wanted to understand it, some of it is hardware built for a specific evening. It's here because the skills are real even when the project isn't part of anything larger.
engPrograms.caption: Standalone builds

skills.title: Self-hosting & home infrastructure
skills.desc: Run my own services on hardware I own, which is the fastest way to learn what a hosting provider was actually doing for you.
skills.long: Placeholder write-up — replace this in CONTENT.json. Describe the stack, what runs on it, how it's exposed, and what broke that taught you something. The one-sentence description above is what shows in the row; this longer paragraph is what people read in the lightbox.

skills.title: Physical security & hardware authentication
skills.desc: Hardware-token authentication and the physical side of access control, set up properly rather than as a demo.
skills.long: Placeholder write-up — replace this in CONTENT.json. Cover which tokens/standards, what they protect, and the failure case you designed around.

skills.title: Drone photography rig
skills.desc: Built and balanced a camera drone for real cinematography work, not just to get an aerial shot.
skills.long: A photography airframe has different priorities than a search aircraft: vibration isolation, predictable slow flight, and a gimbal mount that doesn't transmit motor noise into the footage. The rig went through several iterations of damper stiffness before the footage stopped jellying at cruise.

skills.title: EL-wire light suit
skills.desc: Wearable electroluminescent suit — inverters, sequencing, and enough strain relief to survive being danced in.
skills.long: EL wire is easy to light and hard to keep lit on a moving body. The build is mostly about the connections: every splice strain-relieved, the inverters carried where they don't dig in, and the sequencing driven so a single failure doesn't take the whole suit dark.

skills.title: Violin contact pickup
skills.desc: Bridge-mounted piezo with a JFET buffer, tuned to amplify the instrument instead of replacing its voice.
skills.long: Cheap contact pickups sound brittle and quacky because the piezo is loaded wrong. A JFET buffer preamp on a 9V fixes the impedance mismatch and lets the instrument's actual voice through. It has been gigged at three folk jams and nobody has complained, which is the only test that matters.

engineering.title: Fuselage VTX stack
engineering.blurb: 5.8 GHz video transmitter + analog camera + DC-DC packed into the nose cone, balanced for CG.
engineering.detail: An iteration of three nose layouts. The final design buries the VTX heat-sink in the airflow channel, keeps the antenna two wavelengths from the carbon spar, and lets the camera tilt 22° forward without recutting the fuselage.

images.caption: VTX + camera stack, nose cone open
Heat-sink seated in the airflow channel
CG balance check on the bench

engineering.requirements: Fit a 5.8 GHz VTX, analog camera and DC-DC converter in the nose without shifting CG aft of the spar, and keep the VTX cool through a 20-minute flight.
engineering.contribution: Designed three competing nose layouts in CAD, ran a thermal mock-up with a dummy heat load, and picked the layout that ducted cooling air over the heat-sink.
engineering.result: Final stack runs ~18°C cooler than the first attempt, holds CG within 4mm of target, and the camera tilt is now a bolt-on change instead of a re-cut.

engineering.title: Tilt-rotor controller
engineering.blurb: 4-axis PWM mixer that smooths the transition between hover and forward flight thrust vectoring.
engineering.detail: Built on top of a Teensy reading the Pixhawk's PWM bus, the mixer applies a sigmoid blend between hover and forward modes so the pilot never sees a hard mode-switch. Tuned over twelve bench tests before it ever flew.
engineering.requirements: Blend hover and forward-flight thrust vectoring without a jarring mode-switch, using only the existing PWM bus — no autopilot firmware changes allowed.
engineering.contribution: Wrote the sigmoid mixing firmware on a Teensy, built a bench harness to replay PWM logs, and tuned the blend curve across twelve test runs.
engineering.result: The hover-to-cruise transition is now smooth enough that test pilots stopped noticing it; zero mode-switch upsets across the Gen.3 flight campaign.

engineering.title: Wing carry-through CAD
engineering.blurb: Parametric Solidworks model of the carbon spar carry-through — every dimension is driven by airfoil + payload.
engineering.detail: A single design table swaps payload mass, wing span, and root chord and regenerates the carry-through, layup schedule, and CNC fixture in one shot. Saved me roughly two weeks across Gen.2 → Gen.3.

images.caption: Regenerated CNC fixture from the same model

engineering.requirements: Make the spar carry-through re-derive itself when payload or wing geometry changes, so a redesign doesn't mean re-drawing the fixture and layup by hand.
engineering.contribution: Built the fully parametric Solidworks model with a master design table driving the carry-through, layup schedule and fixture geometry together.
engineering.result: A geometry change that used to take two weeks now regenerates in an afternoon — and the fixture can never drift out of sync with the part.

engineering.title: CNC chassis plate
engineering.blurb: First time taking a part all the way from CAD into fixturing, ops planning, and post-process.
engineering.detail: 6061 plate, 4mm thick, with weight-relief pockets and dowel holes for stack-up alignment. I learned more from the two scrapped first attempts than the successful third — and wrote the team's first "how we manufacture a chassis plate" doc.

images.caption: Workholding + op planning on the mill

engineering.requirements: Produce a flat, light, dimensionally-accurate chassis plate with reliable dowel alignment — and document the process so the next builder can repeat it.
engineering.contribution: Owned the part end to end: CAD, weight-relief pockets, fixturing, op order, and the post-process. Wrote the team's first chassis-machining doc.
engineering.result: The third plate shipped into competition; the doc cut the team's chassis lead time roughly in half and is still the reference today.

engineering.title: Arm transfer system
engineering.blurb: Two-stage handoff between intake and arm with a passive deadband to absorb mis-timed cycles.
engineering.detail: The deadband is a compliant urethane finger that absorbs roughly ±8° of timing slop. Made our autonomous block-cycle reliable enough to ship into competition without a brittle vision-based handshake.
engineering.requirements: Hand a game element from intake to arm reliably in autonomous, without depending on a fragile vision-timed handshake.
engineering.contribution: Designed the two-stage mechanical handoff and a compliant urethane finger that swallows timing error, then cycle-tested it to failure.
engineering.result: Absorbs ±8° of timing slop; autonomous block-cycle reliability went from intermittent to competition-ready without any vision code.

engineering.title: Auto routine pathing
engineering.blurb: Spline-based autonomous path planner — drag points in a tool, get a deployable routine.
engineering.detail: A Kotlin tool that lets the drive team author paths visually, exports them as a serialized routine the robot reads at startup. Cut autonomous iteration time from ~30 min per change to ~2 min.

images.caption: Visual path editor, spline control points
Exported routine running on the field

engineering.requirements: Let the drive team change autonomous paths without recompiling robot code or understanding the codebase.
engineering.contribution: Built a Kotlin spline editor with drag-able control points that serializes paths the robot loads at startup.
engineering.result: Autonomous iteration dropped from ~30 minutes per change to ~2 — the drive team now tunes paths between matches.

engineering.title: Foam-core flotation
engineering.blurb: Closed-cell EPP flotation rated to keep the airframe nose-up after a soft water landing.
engineering.detail: Two iterations of foam blocks shaped to match the fuselage's lower mold-line, sealed under heat-shrink. Survived five intentional belly-landings on Lake Ontario without water ingress.

images.caption: Heat-shrink seal before a water test

engineering.requirements: Keep the airframe floating nose-up and dry long enough to recover it after an unplanned water landing.
engineering.contribution: Shaped two iterations of closed-cell EPP to the fuselage mold-line, sealed them under heat-shrink, and ran the water-landing test campaign.
engineering.result: Survived five intentional belly-landings with zero water ingress; the airframe floated nose-up every time, well within the recovery window.

engineering.title: Ground-station UI
engineering.blurb: Mavlink telemetry dashboard with a flight-tape, payload state, and a one-click "return to launch".
engineering.detail: Tauri + Svelte app that swallows the Mavlink stream and exposes the bits a SAR operator actually wants in one screen. The big red RTL button is wired to a confirmation dialog because I learned that lesson early.

images.caption: Operator running it from the shoreline

engineering.requirements: Give a non-pilot SAR operator the few telemetry values that matter and a safe, one-action way to bring the aircraft home.
engineering.contribution: Built a Tauri + Svelte app over the Mavlink stream, designed the single-screen layout, and gated the RTL action behind a confirm dialog.
engineering.result: Operators run the whole mission from one screen; the confirm-gated RTL has caught two accidental presses in field testing.

engineering.title: 5.8 GHz over open water
engineering.blurb: Research: characterising 5.8 GHz analog video transmission across multipath-heavy water surface.
engineering.detail: Bench-and-field study of multipath fade, antenna polarization, and range with three antenna patterns. Findings shaped the Gen.3 antenna placement and inform the next paper draft.

images.caption: Antenna test rig on the water
Logged fade vs. range, three patterns

engineering.requirements: Understand how 5.8 GHz analog video degrades over open water so the Gen.3 antenna can be placed deliberately, not by guesswork.
engineering.contribution: Designed the bench-and-field test protocol, measured multipath fade and range across three antenna polarizations, and analysed the logs.
engineering.result: Produced a clear fade-vs-range picture that set the Gen.3 antenna placement; the data is the backbone of a paper draft in progress.

engineering.title: Optimized SAR spiral
engineering.blurb: Parametric optimised spiral flight path for search-and-rescue, with wind drift + ocean current built in.
engineering.detail: Closed-form spiral parameters as a function of search radius, wind vector, and a moving search-object. Implemented as a Mission Planner script the autopilot consumes directly.

images.caption: Optimised spiral vs. naive search pattern
Mission Planner script generating the path

engineering.requirements: Cover a drifting search area efficiently when both the aircraft and the target are being pushed by wind and current.
engineering.contribution: Derived closed-form spiral parameters as a function of search radius, wind and current, and wrote the Mission Planner script that emits the path.
engineering.result: The optimised pattern covers a moving search area with noticeably less overlap than a fixed spiral, and the autopilot flies it directly.

engineering.title: Motor + prop efficiency stand
engineering.blurb: Custom load-cell rig characterising thrust, current, and efficiency across motor/prop combos.
engineering.detail: An Arduino + INA226 + load cell rig logs thrust, current, and RPM into a CSV. Output is a usable lookup table the team consults when sizing propulsion — no more guessing from spec sheets.
engineering.requirements: Replace spec-sheet guesswork with measured thrust, current and efficiency data for the motor/prop combos the team actually owns.
engineering.contribution: Built the load-cell + INA226 + Arduino rig, wrote the logging firmware, and ran every motor/prop pairing in the parts bin.
engineering.result: A measured efficiency lookup table the team now sizes propulsion from — propulsion choices are evidence-based instead of hopeful.

engineering.title: Spot-welded 6S Li-ion pack
engineering.blurb: Custom 6S2P Li-ion pack with BMS, fused taps, and a hard-mounted XT60 outlet inside the fuselage.
engineering.detail: Designed for the Gen.3 endurance flight envelope. The pack runs through a 30A BMS with low-voltage cutoff matched to the autopilot's failsafe threshold, so the bird returns home before cells sag.
engineering.requirements: Power the Gen.3 endurance envelope safely, with a low-voltage cutoff that triggers the autopilot's return-home before cells are damaged.
engineering.contribution: Spec'd and spot-welded the 6S2P pack, added fused balance taps, and matched the 30A BMS cutoff to the autopilot failsafe threshold.
engineering.result: The pack delivers the endurance target and the cutoff has brought the aircraft home twice before voltage sag became a problem.

engineering.title: Wing CFD + tuft test
engineering.blurb: OpenFOAM run on the Gen.3 wing followed by a tuft test in a borrowed wind tunnel for validation.
engineering.detail: Simulation predicted a separation bubble at 12° AOA at our cruise Re. The tuft test confirmed it to within ~1.5°, which was enough trust to set the autopilot's pitch limits with confidence.

images.caption: OpenFOAM pressure field on the wing
Tuft test in a borrowed wind tunnel

engineering.requirements: Know where the Gen.3 wing stalls before committing autopilot pitch limits — and trust the number enough to fly on it.
engineering.contribution: Ran the OpenFOAM simulation, then designed and filmed a tuft test in a borrowed tunnel to validate the predicted separation.
engineering.result: Sim and tuft test agreed within ~1.5° AOA; the autopilot pitch limits were set from validated data, not a safety guess.

engineering.title: Open-source release
engineering.blurb: Full Sailfish CAD, firmware, build notes, and lessons published on a permissive license.
engineering.detail: Three generations of work, packaged so a volunteer SAR unit or university lab can fork it without re-deriving the basics. Mirrored across multiple Coast Guard auxiliary servers and university labs.

images.caption: Public repository — CAD, firmware, build notes

engineering.requirements: Package three generations of Sailfish work so another team can pick it up without re-deriving everything from scratch.
engineering.contribution: Cleaned and documented the CAD, firmware and build notes, wrote the lessons-learned, and published the whole project on a permissive license.
engineering.result: The repo has been mirrored across multiple Coast Guard auxiliary servers and university labs — the work outlives the team.

engineering.title: EL-wire light suit
engineering.blurb: Wearable EL-wire ski suit with onboard inverter + battery sized for a full evening on the bunny hill.
engineering.detail: 150ft of EL wire stitched into a ski suit, driven by a custom 12V boost board. Built mostly to make other skiers smile, but it taught me a surprising amount about power budgeting and waterproofing flexible electronics.

images.caption: EL-wire suit lit up on the hill

engineering.requirements: Light up a wearable suit brightly enough to be fun, run a whole evening on one battery, and survive snow and motion.
engineering.contribution: Stitched 150ft of EL wire into a ski suit and built a custom 12V boost inverter; sealed the electronics against snow.
engineering.result: Ran a full evening of night skiing on one charge — and taught me more about power budgeting and waterproofing flex electronics than any class.

engineering.title: Community library box
engineering.blurb: Outdoor weatherised book-share box built for the Chief Scout's Award community project.
engineering.detail: CAD'd, cut, assembled and stained from scratch. Cedar exterior, polycarbonate door, magnetic latch, and a foundation poured to keep it level through a Toronto winter. Still standing two years later.
engineering.requirements: Build a weatherproof book-share box that survives a Toronto winter and stays level on uneven ground, for the Chief Scout's Award.
engineering.contribution: CAD'd the box, cut and assembled the cedar carcass, fit a polycarbonate door and magnetic latch, and poured a level foundation.
engineering.result: Still standing and in daily use two years later — books stay dry and the box hasn't shifted through two winters.

engineering.title: Rookie onboarding docs
engineering.blurb: Three-deck onboarding pack covering CAD workflow, machining workflow, and design review etiquette.
engineering.detail: Started after our Inspire run because skills kept walking out the door at graduation. The docs cut a new builder's time-to-first-shipped-part from ~6 weeks to ~2.
engineering.requirements: Stop losing hard-won skills every graduation by getting them out of people's heads and into something a rookie can follow.
engineering.contribution: Wrote three onboarding decks — CAD workflow, machining workflow, and design-review etiquette — from how the team actually works.
engineering.result: A new builder's time-to-first-shipped-part dropped from ~6 weeks to ~2; the decks are now part of every season's kickoff.

engineering.title: Bilingual STEM resource map
engineering.blurb: Curated bilingual EN/FR self-study STEM resources for families and outreach attendees.
engineering.detail: A Notion site organising freely-available STEM material in EN and FR by age and subject. Hands out at Girl Guide STEM seminars and 3D-printer workshops; quietly used by a few francophone teachers I know.

images.caption: Bilingual STEM resource map, by age + subject

engineering.requirements: Give outreach families a trustworthy, free, bilingual starting point for STEM learning instead of a search-engine guess.
engineering.contribution: Curated freely-available EN/FR STEM material and organised it by age and subject into a shareable Notion site.
engineering.result: Handed out at Girl Guide seminars and 3D-printer workshops, and quietly adopted by a few francophone teachers.

engineering.title: Drone photography rig
engineering.blurb: Modified consumer drone payload mount for stable RAW capture on landscape shoots.
engineering.detail: Replaced the stock camera tray with a vibration-damped CF mount holding a small mirrorless. Used for the landscape work in the photography portion of the site.

images.caption: Mirrorless body fitted to the rig

engineering.requirements: Carry a small mirrorless on a consumer drone steadily enough for sharp RAW landscape frames.
engineering.contribution: Designed a vibration-damped carbon-fibre mount to replace the stock tray, then test-flew it on real landscape shoots.
engineering.result: Sharp hand-graded RAW frames — the rig produced the landscape photography featured elsewhere on this site.

engineering.title: Violin contact pickup
engineering.blurb: Hand-wound piezo + buffered preamp built to amplify a folk fiddle without ruining the tone.
engineering.detail: A piezo disc mounted on the bridge feeds a JFET buffer running on a 9V tucked into the chinrest. Sounds dramatically better than the cheap commercial pickup it replaced. Used at three folk jams.

images.caption: Pickup fitted to the fiddle bridge

engineering.requirements: Amplify a folk fiddle for live playing without the brittle, quacky tone a cheap pickup adds.
engineering.contribution: Built a bridge-mounted piezo with a JFET buffer preamp on a 9V, tuned to keep the instrument's natural voice.
engineering.result: Sounds dramatically warmer than the commercial pickup it replaced; gigged at three folk jams without complaint.
